title: Future continuous and future perfect
objectives: Form future continuous and future perfect statements and questions.
Distinguish future progress from completion by a reference time.
Recognise future necessity with will have to.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: The future continuous presents an activity as being in progress at a future time: ‘At ten tomorrow, I'll be meeting a client’. It looks at the activity from a point within it. The sentence does not say exactly when the meeting will start or finish.

The future perfect presents an event as completed before or by a future reference point: ‘By ten tomorrow, I'll have finished the report’. It looks back from that future point to the completion. Both forms describe a future viewpoint, but one foregrounds progress and the other foregrounds completion before a deadline or reference time.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Form the future continuous with will be plus an -ing form: ‘She will be working’. Form the future perfect with will have plus a past participle: ‘She will have finished’. In questions, put will before the subject: ‘Will she be working?’ and ‘Will she have finished?’ Negatives use will not or won't before be or have.

Time expressions help establish the viewpoint. At ten tomorrow often identifies a point at which an activity is in progress. By ten means no later than that time and often accompanies the future perfect: ‘By ten, they will have left’. The time expression alone does not mechanically decide the form; the intended meaning matters.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘At noon, I will be writing the report’ with ‘By noon, I will have written the report’. The first presents the writing as in progress at noon. The second presents it as complete no later than noon. We can also use a duration with the future perfect: ‘By June, she will have worked here for five years’.

The future continuous can make a neutral enquiry about an expected activity: ‘Will you be using the meeting room this afternoon?’ Depending on tone and context, this can sound less like a direct request than ‘Will you use the room?’. It can also describe an event expected as part of the normal course of things.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not confuse the structure will have plus a participle with will have to plus a base verb. ‘I will have finished’ predicts completion; ‘I will have to finish’ expresses future necessity. Use the participle after will have: ‘will have written’, not ‘will have wrote’.

Do not infer that every use of the future continuous is an arrangement or that every deadline requires the future perfect. A speaker can say ‘I'll finish by noon’ as well as ‘I'll have finished by noon’. In controlled exercises, follow the specified focus or form when more than one grammatical choice is possible.

examples.sentence: At ten tomorrow, I'll be meeting a client.
examples.note: The future continuous presents the activity as in progress.

examples.sentence: By ten, I'll have finished the report.
examples.note: The future perfect presents completion by ten.

examples.sentence: At noon, they will be travelling.
examples.note: The activity is viewed from a future point within it.

examples.sentence: By noon, they will have arrived.
examples.note: The arrival is presented as complete by noon.

examples.sentence: Will you be using the room this afternoon?
examples.note: The future continuous can make a neutral enquiry.

examples.sentence: By June, she will have worked here for five years.
examples.note: The future perfect can describe a period up to a future point.

examples.sentence: She won't have finished by five.
examples.note: Won't makes the future perfect negative.

examples.sentence: I will have to finish tomorrow.
examples.note: Have to expresses necessity, not the future perfect.

common_errors.incorrect: She will be work at ten.
common_errors.correct: She will be working at ten.
common_errors.reason: Use an -ing form after will be in the future continuous.

common_errors.incorrect: They will have wrote it by noon.
common_errors.correct: They will have written it by noon.
common_errors.reason: Use the participle written after will have.

common_errors.incorrect: Will she have finished? Yes, she has.
common_errors.correct: Will she have finished? Yes, she will.
common_errors.reason: Use will in the short answer to this will question.

summary: Use will be plus -ing to present an activity in progress at a future point.
Use will have plus a past participle to present completion by a future point.
Distinguish will have finished from will have to finish.

option_feedback.d: “I have finished.” does not fit here. Will have to finish expresses necessity.
